story.title: Meera and the colour of the stars

scenes.text: On a clear night Meera notices that Betelgeuse looks orange-red while Rigel looks blue-white.
Her physics teacher says: colour is a thermometer. The hotter the surface, the shorter the wavelength where it glows brightest.

steps.title: Blackbody radiation
steps.body: A star is close to an ideal **blackbody**: an object whose emission depends only on its temperature T. Its spectrum has one peak. **Wien's displacement law** gives the peak wavelength: **λmax = b / T**, with b = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · The Sun's peak colour
steps.body:
T = 5772 K.
- λmax = 2.898×10⁻³ / 5772 = 5.02×10⁻⁷ m
- = **502 nm**, in the green part of the visible spectrum.

The Sun looks white-yellow because it emits across the whole visible band, not only at its peak.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · A hot O-type star
steps.body: T = 20 000 K gives λmax = 2.898×10⁻³ / 20000 = 1.449×10⁻⁷ m = **145 nm**, in the ultraviolet. Most of its energy is invisible to us, yet it still looks blue because its visible tail is steeper on the blue side.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Celsius instead of kelvin.
- Thinking the peak wavelength is "the colour we see".
- Forgetting that λmax is shorter for hotter bodies (inverse relation).

steps.title: Stefan–Boltzmann law
steps.body: Power radiated per unit area is σT⁴ with σ = 5.670×10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. For a spherical star: **L = 4πR²σT⁴**. Scaling to the Sun: **L/L☉ = (R/R☉)² (T/T☉)⁴**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Luminosity of the Sun
Solved example 2 · A red giant
steps.body:
Star B: R = 10 R☉, T = 4000 K.
- L/L☉ = 10² × (4000/5772)⁴ = 100 × 0.2307 = **23.1**.

It is cooler, but its surface area is 100 times bigger, so it is 23 times brighter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Squaring T instead of raising it to the 4th power.
- Forgetting that area scales as R², not R.
- Mixing solar units with SI units in one formula.

steps.title: Magnitude scale
steps.body: Apparent magnitude m measures brightness as seen from Earth; absolute magnitude M is what it would be at 10 pc. A difference of 5 magnitudes = factor 100 in flux. **Distance modulus: m − M = 5 log₁₀(d/10 pc)**. Smaller numbers mean brighter.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Flux ratio
steps.body: Two stars differ by 5 magnitudes: flux ratio = 100^(5/5) = **100**. One magnitude is a factor 2.512.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using d in light-years without converting (1 pc = 3.26 ly).
- Forgetting the scale is inverted: a magnitude 1 star is brighter than magnitude 6.
- Ignoring interstellar extinction for distant stars.

courses.title: Stars II · Birth, life and death of stars
courses.summary: The H–R diagram, main-sequence lifetimes, how stars of different mass end as white dwarfs, neutron stars or black holes, and where the heavy elements come from.
outcomes: Read the H–R diagram and locate stellar stages

lessons.title: The H–R diagram and the main sequence

scenes.text: Meera plots 200 nearby stars by temperature and luminosity.
Most fall on a diagonal band. A few sit above it, a few below. Each position is a life stage.

steps.title: Hertzsprung–Russell diagram
steps.body: Plot luminosity (vertical) against surface temperature (horizontal, **hot on the left**). Regions: **main sequence** (hydrogen fusing in the core, ~90% of stars), **red giants/supergiants** (upper right), **white dwarfs** (lower left).

steps.title: Why mass decides everything
steps.body: Mass sets core pressure and temperature, thus the fusion rate. More massive stars are far more luminous, roughly **L ∝ M^3.5** on the main sequence, so they burn their fuel faster.

steps.title: Solved example · Luminosity of a 2 M☉ star
steps.body: L ≈ 2^3.5 = 11.3 L☉. Fuel available ∝ M = 2, so lifetime ∝ M/L = M^−2.5 → 2^−2.5 = 0.177 of the Sun's ~10 Gyr = **1.77 Gyr**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading the temperature axis left-to-right as increasing; it is reversed.
- Thinking big stars live longer because they have more fuel.
- Treating L ∝ M^3.5 as exact; it is an approximation for roughly 2–50 M☉ range.

scenes.text: Meera must write a leaflet titled "How stars die" for her college science club.
She lists remnants: white dwarf, neutron star, black hole.

steps.title: End states
steps.body:
- **Low and intermediate mass (up to ~8 M☉ initially):** shed envelope as a planetary nebula, leaving a **white dwarf** supported by electron degeneracy pressure.
- **Chandrasekhar limit ≈ 1.4 M☉:** a white dwarf above this cannot be supported.
- **Massive stars:** iron core collapses, a **core-collapse supernova**, leaving a **neutron star** or **black hole**.

steps.title: Solved example · Schwarzschild radius
steps.body: R = 2GM/c². For M = 1.989×10³⁰ kg: 2×6.674×10⁻¹¹×1.989×10³⁰/(2.998×10⁸)² = **2.95 km**. Compressed inside this radius, the Sun would be a black hole.

steps.title: Origin of elements
steps.body: Fusion makes elements up to iron; heavier elements come from neutron capture processes in supernovae and neutron-star mergers. The iron in blood and the calcium in bones were made in stars.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Sun will become a black hole; it will become a white dwarf.
- Believing black holes "suck in" everything; far away their gravity is the same as any mass.

scenes.text: Meera reads that a space telescope found a planet that goes round its star in 8 years.
How far out is it? Kepler's third law answers.

steps.title: Three laws
steps.body: 1) Orbits are **ellipses** with the star at one focus. 2) A line from star to planet sweeps **equal areas in equal times**. 3) **P² = a³** when P is in years and a in AU (for a one-solar-mass star). Newton generalised to P² = 4π²a³/(GM).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: a = 4 AU: P = √(4³) = √64 = **8 years**. Reverse: P = 8 yr → a = 8^(2/3) = 4 AU.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the formula P² = a³ with days or km.
- Applying it unchanged to stars of different mass without the factor M.

steps.title: Radial velocity
steps.body: A planet and star orbit their common centre of mass; the star wobbles, shifting spectral lines by the Doppler effect. Large, close-in planets give the biggest signals.

steps.title: Together
steps.body: Transit gives radius, RV gives minimum mass; combined they give density (rocky vs gas). Direct imaging suits young, wide, hot giants.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Radius = 2 R⊕ and mass = 5 M⊕: density relative to Earth = 5/2³ = **0.625** of Earth's ~5.5 g/cm³ ≈ 3.4 g/cm³, a likely volatile-rich super-Earth or mini-Neptune.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling RV mass the true mass; it is M sin i.
- Assuming every dip is a planet (eclipsing binaries cause false positives).

courses.summary: Hubble's law, redshift, the cosmic microwave background, the age and fate of the Universe, and the evidence for dark matter and dark energy at an introductory undergraduate level.

scenes.text: Meera reads that distant galaxies recede faster than near ones.
No galaxy is at the centre: space itself expands, like dots on an inflating balloon.

steps.title: Redshift
steps.body: z = (λobs − λemit)/λemit. For small z, **v ≈ c z**. Cosmological redshift is stretching of light by expanding space.

steps.title: Hubble's law
steps.body: **v = H0 d**, with H0 ≈ 70 km/s/Mpc (measurements range ~67–73 km/s/Mpc; this "Hubble tension" is an open problem).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the expansion as galaxies flying through space.
- Using v = cz at large z (needs relativistic or cosmological formula).
- Mixing Mpc with light-years.

lessons.title: The CMB and the Big Bang evidence

scenes.text: A radio receiver picks up a faint, nearly uniform glow from all directions.
It matches a blackbody of 2.725 K.

steps.title: Three pillars
steps.body: 1) Hubble expansion. 2) The **cosmic microwave background**, released ~380 000 years after the Big Bang when atoms formed; today a 2.725 K blackbody. 3) **Primordial abundances**: ~75% H and ~25% He by mass, matching Big-Bang nucleosynthesis predictions.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · CMB peak
steps.body: λmax = 2.898×10⁻³/2.725 = **1.06 mm**, in the microwave band.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Hubble time
steps.body: 1/H0 = 977.8/70 = **13.97 Gyr**; the actual age ~13.8 Gyr is close because expansion rate has changed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Big Bang was an explosion at a point in space.
- Confusing the CMB redshift (z ≈ 1100) with galaxy redshifts.

scenes.text: Meera meets three puzzling observations at a seminar.

steps.title: Dark matter
steps.body: Galaxy rotation curves stay flat and clusters bend light more than visible mass allows (gravitational lensing). Something unseen provides extra gravity.

steps.title: Dark energy
steps.body: Supernova Ia observations in the late 1990s showed distant supernovae fainter than expected: expansion is accelerating. In the standard ΛCDM model, roughly 5% is ordinary matter, ~27% dark matter and ~68% dark energy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling dark matter "dark" because it is black; it simply does not emit or absorb light.
- Treating ΛCDM percentages as settled forever; they are best-fit values.

courses.summary: An overview of India's space programme — satellites, lunar, Mars and solar missions — with the physics of rockets: the Tsiolkovsky equation, orbital velocity and why multi-stage rockets work.
outcomes: Describe the main categories of ISRO missions without memorising dates

lessons.title: India's space programme at a glance

story.title: From a bicycle to the Moon

scenes.text: Early Indian rocket parts were carried on bicycles and bullock carts to a fishing village launch site.
Today India launches its own satellites and has reached the Moon and Mars orbit.

steps.title: Missions by purpose
steps.body:
- **Earth observation and communication:** INSAT, GSAT, IRS/Resourcesat, Cartosat families that support weather, broadcasting, mapping and agriculture. NavIC is India's regional navigation system.
- **Science:** AstroSat (multi-wavelength space observatory) and Aditya-L1 (solar observatory at the Sun–Earth L1 point).
- **Planetary:** Chandrayaan-1 (lunar orbiter), Mangalyaan/Mars Orbiter Mission (reached Mars orbit on its first attempt) and Chandrayaan-3 (landed near the Moon's south polar region in August 2023).
- **Launchers:** PSLV (workhorse), GSLV and LVM3 for heavier payloads.

steps.title: Why L1?
steps.body: The L1 point lies about 1.5 million km from Earth towards the Sun, where gravity of Sun and Earth balances orbital motion so a spacecraft can keep an uninterrupted view of the Sun.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up Chandrayaan-1 (orbiter), -2 (orbiter plus lander that failed to land softly) and -3 (successful soft landing).
- Saying Mangalyaan landed on Mars; it orbited.
- Quoting costs and dates without checking official ISRO sources.

story.title: Why the mountain air is thin

scenes.text: Ravi climbs to 5.5 km on a Himalayan trek; his phone barometer reads about half of sea-level pressure.
Why?

steps.title: Layers
steps.body: Troposphere (weather, to ~12 km average; temperature falls ~6.5 °C/km), stratosphere (ozone layer, temperature rises), mesosphere, thermosphere. About 80% of mass is in the troposphere.

steps.title: Pressure law
steps.body: p = p0 exp(−z/H) with scale height H ≈ 8.4 km (isothermal approximation).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying air is thin because gravity is weaker; it is thin because less air lies above.
- Treating the formula as exact in a real atmosphere.

steps.title: Coriolis
steps.body: f = 2Ω sin φ with Ω = 7.292×10⁻⁵ rad/s. f = 0 at the equator, largest at the poles. In the northern hemisphere deflection is to the right.

steps.title: Wind patterns
steps.body: Balance of pressure gradient and Coriolis gives **geostrophic wind** parallel to isobars. Northern hemisphere: **anticlockwise** inflow around lows, **clockwise** around highs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing cyclones near the equator form easily; f≈0 means too little spin.
- Reversing the direction in the southern hemisphere.

courses.title: Meteorology II · The Indian monsoon
courses.summary: Why India has a monsoon: land–sea heating, the ITCZ shift, Tibetan Plateau, jets and low-pressure systems, onset and withdrawal, breaks, the IMD rainfall categories and ENSO/IOD links.
outcomes: Classify seasonal rainfall by IMD categories

scenes.text: Around 1 June the monsoon typically arrives over Kerala.
The sea breeze of summer becomes continental-scale.

steps.title: Mechanism
steps.body: Land heats faster than the ocean, producing a thermal low over northwest India and Pakistan (the heat low). The **ITCZ** moves north (~20–25°N over the Gangetic plain). Southeast trade winds cross the equator, are deflected to the right by Coriolis and become the **southwest monsoon**, carrying moisture from the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal.

steps.title: Other players
steps.body: The **Tibetan Plateau** is a high-level heat source; the **Somali (Findlater) jet** is a low-level cross-equatorial jet; the **tropical easterly jet** aloft; Western Ghats cause orographic rain; **monsoon trough** and Bay of Bengal low-pressure systems bring rain to central and north India.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Describing the monsoon as a single rain event instead of a seasonal wind reversal.
- Saying the monsoon only starts from the Bay; branches exist in both seas.

steps.title: Balance
steps.body: Incoming sunlight S = 1361 W/m² on a surface facing the Sun. Averaged over the sphere, divide by 4. Albedo α ≈ 0.30. Balance: S(1−α)/4 = σT⁴.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Absorbed = 1361 × 0.7/4 = **238 W/m²**. T = (238.2/5.670×10⁻⁸)^(1/4) = **254.6 K ≈ −18.6 °C**. Observed mean ≈ 288 K, so the natural greenhouse effect warms by about **33 K**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Celsius in σT⁴.
- Forgetting the division by 4 (disc vs sphere).
- Saying the greenhouse effect is bad in itself; the natural one keeps Earth habitable.

scenes.text: Ravi picks up a glassy, six-sided crystal from a stream bed near Rajasthan's hills.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: A mineral is a **naturally occurring, inorganic, crystalline solid with a definite (but variable within limits) chemical composition**. Coal and glass are not minerals.

steps.title: Mohs scale of hardness
steps.body: 1 talc, 2 gypsum, 3 calcite, 4 fluorite, 5 apatite, 6 orthoclase feldspar, 7 quartz, 8 topaz, 9 corundum, 10 diamond. A fingernail is ~2.5, a copper coin ~3, a steel nail ~5.5, window glass ~5.5.

steps.title: Solved example · Field test
steps.body: A mineral scratches glass and is not scratched by a steel nail → hardness > 5.5, ≈ 6.5–7; with a vitreous lustre and hexagonal prisms this suggests **quartz**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing hardness (resistance to scratching) with toughness.
- Judging colour alone: quartz comes in many colours.
- Testing streak on a mineral harder than the streak plate.

steps.title: Igneous

- Forgetting texture depends on cooling rate, not composition.

steps.title: Sedimentary
steps.body: Weathering → erosion → transport → deposition → burial and **lithification**. Clastic (sandstone, shale), chemical/biochemical (limestone, rock salt). Contain fossils and layers (bedding).

steps.title: Metamorphic
steps.body: Altered by heat, pressure or fluids without melting. Limestone → marble, sandstone → quartzite, shale → slate → schist → gneiss. Foliation shows directed pressure.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: A banded coarse rock with alternating light and dark minerals = **gneiss**, high-grade.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Saying metamorphism involves melting.
- Thinking fossils survive in high-grade metamorphic rocks.

steps.title: Solved example · Which rock next?
steps.body: Granite uplifted and weathered gives sand and clay; buried and cemented these become **sandstone and shale**; heat and pressure convert them into **quartzite and slate**. Each arrow in the cycle needs a specific process.

steps.title: Cycle
steps.body: Magma → igneous → weathering → sediment → sedimentary → heat/pressure → metamorphic → melting → magma. Many shortcuts exist: any rock can be uplifted and weathered.

steps.title: Solved example · Shortcuts
steps.body: Metamorphic rock can be uplifted and weathered straight into sediment without ever melting; igneous rock can be metamorphosed by a later intrusion. The cycle has many shortcuts.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the cycle as a one-way circle.
- Forgetting that burial and heating are slow: millions of years.

steps.title: Waves
steps.body: **P (primary)** compressional, fastest, travels through solids and liquids. **S (secondary)** shear, slower, solids only. **Surface waves (Love, Rayleigh)** slowest but most damaging.

steps.title: S–P method
steps.body: Distance d = Δt × (vp·vs)/(vp − vs). With vp = 6.0 km/s and vs = 3.5 km/s the factor is 6×3.5/2.5 = **8.4 km per second of lag**. Three stations → three circles → epicentre.

steps.body:

- Using only one station: it gives distance, not direction.

steps.title: Magnitude vs intensity

steps.title: Product rule
steps.body: Genotype frequency = 2pq for heterozygotes, p² for homozygotes. Independent loci multiply.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Genotype frequencies 0.10, 0.05, 0.20, 0.08 → product = **8×10⁻⁵ = 1 in 12 500**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A heterozygote with p = 0.1, q = 0.2: 2pq = **0.04**.

steps.title: Fallacy
steps.body: The match probability is **not** the probability of innocence. "Only 1 in 12 500 would match" ≠ "the chance he is innocent is 1 in 12 500", especially in a large city.

steps.body: Dendrites receive, soma integrates, axon hillock initiates the spike, axon conducts, terminals release neurotransmitter. Glia (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes making CNS myelin, microglia) support and protect. Schwann cells myelinate in the PNS.

steps.title: Gradients

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Assuming the pump directly produces the spike; ion channels do that.

steps.title: Nernst
steps.body: E = (RT/zF) ln([out]/[in]). At 37 °C, for monovalent ions, **E ≈ 61.5 mV × log₁₀([out]/[in])**.

steps.title: Resting potential
steps.body: Near −70 mV because the membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺ at rest, but a little Na⁺ leaks in. The Goldman equation weights each ion by permeability.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ln with the 61.5 factor.
- Flipping out/in.
- Forgetting the sign.

steps.title: Spike phases
steps.body: Threshold (~−55 mV) → voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open (rapid depolarisation, overshoot to about +30–40 mV) → Na⁺ channels inactivate and K⁺ channels open (repolarisation) → undershoot (hyperpolarisation) → rest. Absolute refractory period ensures one-way travel. Myelin gives **saltatory conduction** between nodes of Ranvier.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Rule of thumb for myelinated axons: v ≈ 6 m/s per µm of diameter → 10 µm gives ~60 m/s. Time over 1 m = 1/60 = **16.7 ms**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing the spike gets bigger with stronger stimulus (all-or-none).
- Thinking myelin is continuous along the axon.

outcomes: Describe the steps of synaptic transmission

scenes.text: A spike reaches a terminal. Within a millisecond a chemical crosses a gap about 20 nm wide.
The next neuron decides whether to fire.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body: Spike arrives → voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open → Ca²⁺ triggers vesicle fusion (SNARE proteins) → transmitter diffuses across the cleft → binds receptors (ionotropic = fast channels; metabotropic = slower G-protein pathways) → postsynaptic potential → transmitter cleared by reuptake, enzymes or diffusion.

steps.title: EPSP vs IPSP
steps.body: **Excitatory (EPSP)** depolarises toward threshold (glutamate opens Na⁺/Ca²⁺ channels). **Inhibitory (IPSP)** hyperpolarises or shunts (GABA and glycine open Cl⁻ channels). The neuron sums inputs in space and time.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying transmitters cause the spike directly; they change membrane potential which may reach threshold.
- Mistaking botulinum toxin (blocks release) for a receptor blocker.

scenes.text: A neuron rests at −70 mV; threshold is −55 mV.
Each EPSP adds 5 mV and each IPSP subtracts 3 mV.

steps.title: Summation
steps.body: Spatial summation adds inputs from different synapses at once; temporal summation adds rapid inputs from the same synapse.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Needed rise: −55 − (−70) = 15 mV. Five EPSPs give +25 mV; two IPSPs give −6 mV; net +19 mV ≥ 15 → **fires**. With 3 EPSPs and 2 IPSPs net +9 mV → does not fire.

steps.title: Transmitters
steps.body: Acetylcholine: neuromuscular junction and memory/attention systems; dopamine: reward/movement (loss in Parkinson disease); serotonin: mood, sleep, appetite; noradrenaline: arousal; endorphins: pain modulation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling dopamine "the pleasure chemical" simply; it signals reward prediction and motivation.
- Seeking medical conclusions from this overview.

steps.title: Memory systems
steps.body: Sensory → working memory (~4±1 chunks) → long-term. Declarative (episodic, semantic) vs procedural (skills). Consolidation occurs during sleep.

steps.title: LTP
steps.body: **Long-term potentiation**: repeated strong activation strengthens synapses via NMDA receptor-dependent Ca²⁺ entry ("cells that fire together wire together"). A basis for learning.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Simple forgetting model R = e^(−t/S). With S = 5 days after 3 days: R = e^(−0.6) = **0.549**, about 55%. Spaced review raises S, slowing forgetting.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming cramming equals durable learning.
- Treating the exponential model as exact for all material.

steps.title: Defects
steps.body: Point (vacancy, interstitial, substitutional), line (**dislocations**), planar (grain boundaries, stacking faults), volume (voids). steps.body: A **phase** is a physically distinct, homogeneous region. Gibbs phase rule at constant pressure: F = C − P + 1. In a two-phase region of a binary alloy, composition of each phase is read from the tie-line ends.

steps.title: Hazard vs exposure
steps.body: Risk = hazard × exposure. Nanoparticles can reach deep in the lungs, cross some membranes and behave differently from bulk. Needle-like nanotubes raised asbestos-like concerns in some studies. Release into water (nano-silver from textiles) can harm aquatic microbes.

steps.title: Good practice
steps.body: Use fume hoods and appropriate respirators, wet handling, closed systems, waste segregation, life-cycle thinking and the precautionary principle; follow national regulators and standards (for example BIS and CPCB/MoEFCC guidance in India, and international ISO/OECD work).

- Assuming "natural" or "bulk-safe" means nano-safe.
- Stating that nano is dangerous per se; hazard depends on material, shape, dose and coating.
